before.content_html:
The Storm (Act 1, Scene 1)

The play opens with a violent storm at sea — the tempest of the title. Shakespeare plunges the audience into chaos: the Boatswain shouts commands, nobles panic, and the ship breaks apart. The storm immediately establishes a key theme — the disruption and restoration of order. On the ship, social hierarchy collapses: the Boatswain tells the courtiers that "the elements" care nothing for their rank, asking "What cares these roarers for the name of king?"

This challenge to authority is significant. In Jacobean England, the idea that nature could override the power of a king was both thrilling and disturbing. The storm also functions as a pathetic fallacy, reflecting the political chaos caused by Antonio's usurpation of Prospero's dukedom twelve years earlier.

Key Fact

The storm is not natural — it is created by Prospero's magic, performed by Ariel. No one is actually harmed. This reveals Prospero's immense power and his ability to manipulate others through illusion, establishing the theme of art and control.

Prospero's Exposition (Act 1, Scene 2)

Act 1, Scene 2 is the longest scene in the play and serves as the exposition. Prospero tells Miranda their history: he was the rightful Duke of Milan, but his brother Antonio, "in my trust," conspired with Alonso, King of Naples, to overthrow him. Prospero and the infant Miranda were set adrift in a "rotten carcass of a butt" — a barely seaworthy boat — and left to die.

Prospero's account reveals his own flaw: he neglected his ducal duties to study "the liberal arts" and magic, giving Antonio the opportunity to seize power. The phrase "my library / Was dukedom large enough" suggests Prospero valued intellectual power over political responsibility. This self-awareness is important — he is not a simple victim but a character who contributed to his own overthrow.

Miranda's function in this scene is largely as an audience surrogate. She asks questions so Prospero can explain the backstory. However, she is also presented as deeply empathetic: "O, I have suffered / With those that I saw suffer!" Her compassion for the shipwrecked sailors establishes her as the play's moral heart — she represents the natural goodness that Prospero's control sometimes lacks.

Ariel and the Bond of Servitude

Ariel is an airy spirit who serves Prospero. Before Prospero arrived, Ariel was imprisoned in a "cloven pine" by the witch Sycorax for refusing to carry out her "earthy and abhorred commands." Prospero freed Ariel but bound the spirit to serve him in return. When Ariel requests freedom — "Is there more toil?" — Prospero responds with anger and threats, reminding Ariel of the imprisonment and asking "Dost thou forget / From what a torment I did free thee?"

This exchange is morally complex. Prospero freed Ariel from Sycorax's cruelty, but he has replaced one form of servitude with another. Ariel serves willingly but is not free. The promise of liberty — "After two days / I will discharge thee" — keeps Ariel obedient. A postcolonial reading sees Ariel as a colonised subject who cooperates with the coloniser in exchange for eventual freedom, contrasting with Caliban's open resistance.

Key Fact

Ariel and Caliban represent two contrasting responses to Prospero's power: willing service versus rebellious resistance. Shakespeare uses this contrast to explore whether cooperation or defiance is the more effective response to authority.

Caliban's Introduction

Caliban enters cursing: "A southwest blow on ye / And blister you all o'er!" Prospero calls him "poisonous slave" and threatens him with cramps and pinches. Caliban's response reveals the history of their relationship: Prospero arrived, Caliban showed him "all the qualities o' th' isle," and in return Prospero enslaved him. Caliban's bitterest complaint is about language: "You taught me language, and my profit on't / Is I know how to curse."

Yet Shakespeare complicates our sympathy for Caliban. Prospero states that Caliban attempted to "violate / The honour of my child" — an attempted assault on Miranda. This alleged crime is used to justify Caliban's subjugation. Whether we accept this justification depends on our interpretive lens: a Jacobean audience might see it as proof of Caliban's savagery; a modern audience might question whether the coloniser's narrative is trustworthy.

Sycorax never appears in the play, yet her presence haunts it. She is described by Prospero as a "foul witch" whose "sorceries" were terrible. But we only hear Prospero's version. Caliban calls her his mother and claims the island through her. Shakespeare creates an interesting parallel: both Sycorax and Prospero are magicians who arrived on the island from elsewhere. The difference is that Prospero's story is the one we hear.

before.content_html:
Gonzalo’s Utopian Vision (Act 2, Scene 1)

While the shipwrecked nobles explore the island, the elderly counsellor Gonzalo imagines an ideal commonwealth: “No sovereignty — / All things in common nature should produce / Without sweat or endeavour.” He envisions a world without hierarchy, property, or labour. This speech draws on Michel de Montaigne’s essay “Of Cannibals” (1580), which argued that indigenous peoples lived more natural and virtuous lives than Europeans.

Antonio and Sebastian mock Gonzalo mercilessly, but Shakespeare uses the speech to raise serious questions. Is civilisation an improvement on nature, or a corruption of it? The utopian vision is naive — Gonzalo says ‘no sovereignty’ while imagining himself as king of this commonwealth — but it highlights real philosophical debates about power, property, and human nature that connect to the play’s colonial context.

Key Fact

Gonzalo’s utopian speech echoes Montaigne’s “Of Cannibals,” which Shakespeare almost certainly read. The contradiction — imagining a world without sovereignty while placing himself in charge — highlights the impossibility of escaping power structures entirely.

Antonio and Sebastian’s Conspiracy

While others sleep, Antonio tempts Sebastian to murder his brother Alonso, King of Naples, and seize the crown. Antonio’s temptation mirrors his earlier overthrow of Prospero. He argues that the sleeping king is as good as dead: “What a sleep were this / For your advancement!” The plan parallels Macbeth — a sleeping ruler, an ambitious subordinate, a whispered temptation — but here, Ariel intervenes to wake the sleepers before the murder can happen.

Antonio is the play’s most morally unredeemed character. He shows no remorse for overthrowing his brother, and his willingness to repeat the crime suggests that villainy is habitual for him. Significantly, Antonio never speaks in the final scene’s reconciliation — Shakespeare leaves it ambiguous whether he is genuinely reformed or merely silent.

The Antonio-Sebastian conspiracy echoes the murder of Duncan in Macbeth: a sleeping ruler, an ambitious plotter, and a whispered temptation. But Shakespeare changes the outcome. In Macbeth, the murder succeeds and leads to catastrophe. In The Tempest, Ariel prevents it, and the play moves towards forgiveness rather than revenge. This reflects the shift in Shakespeare’s late romances from tragedy to reconciliation.

Caliban’s Rebellion (Act 2, Scene 2 — Act 3, Scene 2)

Caliban encounters Trinculo and Stephano — a jester and a drunken butler — and immediately offers to serve them: “I’ll show thee every fertile inch o’ th’ island; / And I will kiss thy foot. I prithee, be my god.” His willingness to worship Stephano reveals both his desperation and his vulnerability. He trades one master for another, suggesting that the colonised subject cannot easily escape the structures of servitude.

Yet Caliban’s rebellion is also politically motivated. He proposes a plan to kill Prospero: “Why, as I told thee, ’tis a custom with him / I’ th’ afternoon to sleep. There thou mayst brain him.” This is a genuine plot to overthrow the island’s ruler — a third conspiracy alongside Antonio’s usurpation and the Antonio-Sebastian plot. Shakespeare presents political ambition as universal, not limited to the educated or noble.

Key Fact

Three separate groups conspire for power: Antonio overthrew Prospero in the past; Antonio and Sebastian plot against Alonso; Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo plot against Prospero. Shakespeare suggests that the desire for power operates at every level of society.

Caliban’s Poetry

Despite being presented as “savage,” Caliban speaks some of the play’s most beautiful poetry. His famous speech about the island — “Be not afeard. The isle is full of noises, / Sounds, and sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not” — reveals a sensitivity and emotional depth that contradicts Prospero’s characterisation of him as a “thing of darkness.” The speech suggests that Caliban has a profound spiritual connection to the island that the European characters lack.

This is one of Shakespeare’s most important juxtapositions. The character dismissed as subhuman produces the most humane and lyrical language in the play. It forces the audience to question who the real “savages” are — Caliban, who loves the island, or the Europeans who scheme for power on it.

Stephano and Trinculo provide comic relief but also serve a structural purpose. Their bumbling conspiracy to kill Prospero mirrors Antonio’s sophisticated political treachery. By showing ambition at every social level — from dukes to drunken servants — Shakespeare suggests that the desire for power is a fundamental human drive, not a product of education or status. Their distraction by Prospero’s “glistering apparel” (shiny clothes) in Act 4 shows how easily they are manipulated by superficial wealth.

before.content_html:
The Masque (Act 4, Scene 1)

Prospero stages a masque to celebrate Ferdinand and Miranda’s betrothal. The goddesses Iris, Ceres, and Juno descend to bless the couple with prosperity and fertility. The masque is beautiful, orderly, and controlled — a vision of harmony that reflects Prospero’s ideal world. For a Jacobean audience watching at court, the masque within the play would have mirrored the real court masques they enjoyed under James I.

However, the masque is abruptly interrupted when Prospero remembers Caliban’s conspiracy. He dissolves the vision: “Our revels now are ended. These our actors, / As I foretold you, were all spirits and / Are melted into air, into thin air.” The interruption is significant — the perfect world of art cannot survive contact with the messy reality of human plots and ambitions.

Key Fact

Prospero’s “Our revels now are ended” speech compares life to a theatrical performance. “The great globe itself” refers to both the Earth and Shakespeare’s Globe Theatre. Life, like a play, is temporary: “We are such stuff / As dreams are made on, and our little life / Is rounded with a sleep.”

Prospero’s Renunciation of Magic (Act 5, Scene 1)

In his most powerful soliloquy, Prospero catalogues his magical achievements: he has dimmed the sun, raised storms, opened graves, and commanded spirits. Then he renounces it all: “But this rough magic / I here abjure. And when I have required / Some heavenly music — which even now I do — / I’ll break my staff, / Bury it certain fathoms in the earth, / And deeper than did ever plummet sound / I’ll drown my book.”

The renunciation is the play’s turning point. By destroying his staff and book, Prospero gives up the tools of his power. He chooses to be human — limited, mortal, dependent on others — rather than a god-like controller. Many scholars read this as Shakespeare’s own farewell to the theatre: the playwright, like Prospero, surrendering the power to create worlds from words.

The catalyst for Prospero’s decision to forgive comes from an unexpected source: Ariel. The spirit describes the suffering nobles and says: “Your charm so strongly works ’em / That if you now beheld them your affections / Would become tender.” Prospero asks: “Dost thou think so, spirit?” Ariel replies: “Mine would, sir, were I human.” The irony is devastating: a non-human spirit teaches a human about compassion. Prospero responds with his greatest line: “The rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance.”

Forgiveness and Reconciliation (Act 5)

Prospero confronts his enemies one by one. To Alonso, he reveals that Ferdinand is alive and in love with Miranda — a moment of joy that comes only after genuine repentance. To Antonio, he offers a conditional forgiveness: “For you, most wicked sir, whom to call brother / Would even infect my mouth, I do forgive / Thy rankest fault.” The language is hardly warm — ‘infect,’ ‘rankest fault’ — suggesting that forgiveness is a moral choice rather than an emotional impulse.

Caliban is also released. Prospero acknowledges him: “This thing of darkness I / Acknowledge mine.” The line is profoundly ambiguous. Does it mean Prospero claims Caliban as his responsibility? Or does he recognise the darkness within himself? A postcolonial reading sees it as the coloniser finally admitting ownership of the suffering he has caused.

Key Fact

“The rarer action is in virtue than in vengeance” is the play’s moral turning point. Prospero chooses mercy over revenge, forgiveness over punishment. This distinguishes The Tempest from the tragedies: where Hamlet and Macbeth end in death, Prospero’s story ends in release.

The Epilogue

Prospero’s epilogue is one of the most personal moments in Shakespeare. Standing alone on stage, stripped of magic, Prospero addresses the audience: “Now my charms are all o’erthrown, / And what strength I have’s mine own, / Which is most faint.” He asks for the audience’s “indulgence” (applause) to “set me free.” The boundary between character and playwright dissolves: is this Prospero asking for freedom, or Shakespeare asking for one final ovation?

Prospero’s final act is to free Ariel: “Then to the elements / Be free, and fare thou well!” This release fulfils the promise made in Act 1 and completes the play’s pattern of bondage and liberation. Every character moves towards freedom: Ferdinand from his test, Alonso from his guilt, Caliban from servitude, and Ariel from obligation. Only Antonio’s freedom is ambiguous — he is forgiven but shows no sign of being changed.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses Prospero’s line ‘This thing of darkness I acknowledge mine’ to explore the coloniser-colonised relationship.
practice_questions.marks:

A postcolonial reading: the coloniser admits to creating the ‘darkness’ he attributes to the colonised. The line may also reveal Prospero recognising his own capacity for cruelty.
Lower band (1-2): Basic observation that Prospero acknowledges Caliban.

before.content_html:
Prospero — Magician, Father, Coloniser

Prospero is Shakespeare’s most complex authority figure. He is simultaneously a victim (overthrown by his brother), a father (protective of Miranda), a master (controlling Ariel and Caliban), and an artist (creating illusions through magic). His power is immense: he controls the weather, commands spirits, and manipulates every character on the island. Yet by Act 5, he gives it all up.

The central question is whether Prospero is a benevolent ruler or a tyrant. He frees Ariel from Sycorax but binds the spirit to his own service. He teaches Caliban language but enslaves him. He orchestrates his daughter’s love life. His final choice of mercy suggests growth, but his earlier treatment of Caliban is troubling by modern standards.

Key Fact

Prospero’s flaw is acknowledged in the play: he neglected his ducal duties for magic (‘my library was dukedom large enough’), enabling Antonio’s betrayal. His journey involves learning that power must be surrendered, not hoarded.

Caliban — Monster, Slave, Poet

Caliban is the play’s most contested character. Prospero calls him a “savage,” a “thing of darkness,” and a “born devil.” Yet Caliban produces some of the most beautiful poetry in the play. His duality is central to the play’s meaning.

A postcolonial reading positions Caliban as the indigenous inhabitant of the island, displaced and enslaved by Prospero. His claim — “This island’s mine, by Sycorax my mother” — is a statement of indigenous land rights. A Jacobean reading might see Caliban as a warning about uncontrolled nature that requires civilising force. Shakespeare does not resolve this tension; he presents both perspectives.

Ariel is obedient, versatile, and associated with music and air. Unlike Caliban, Ariel cooperates with Prospero and is rewarded with freedom. A colonial reading sees Ariel as the ‘good native’ who assists the coloniser, contrasting with Caliban’s resistance. But Ariel’s desire for freedom is constant — the spirit repeatedly asks when the promised release will come. Ariel’s most significant moment is teaching Prospero about compassion: “Mine would, sir, were I human.”

Ariel and Caliban can be read as two aspects of Prospero’s personality: Ariel represents his creative, artistic side (the power to enchant), while Caliban represents his darker impulses (the desire to control and dominate).

Miranda — Innocence and Compassion

Miranda has lived on the island since infancy and knows nothing of the wider world. Her famous exclamation — “O brave new world, / That has such people in’t!” — is both joyful and ironic. She celebrates the ‘brave new world’ of the courtiers, unaware that these ‘people’ include the men who plotted against her father. Prospero’s response — “’Tis new to thee” — is weary and knowing.

Miranda’s role is to represent natural empathy. She suffers ‘with those that I saw suffer.’ She proposes to Ferdinand. She challenges her father’s authority. She is the play’s moral heart, and her innocence offers hope that the next generation can be better than the last.

Antonio — The Unredeemed

Antonio is the play’s most clearly villainous character. He overthrew his own brother, conspires to kill Alonso, and shows no remorse when confronted. His silence in the final scene is chilling: while Alonso repents, Antonio says nothing. Shakespeare leaves it ambiguous whether Antonio is genuinely forgiven or merely coerced into silence by Prospero’s restored power.

Gonzalo is the play’s most consistently virtuous character. He secretly helped Prospero and Miranda survive their exile by providing food, water, and Prospero’s books. His utopian vision (Act 2) is mocked but reveals genuine idealism. Prospero’s warmest words in Act 5 are reserved for Gonzalo: “Holy Gonzalo, honourable man.” He represents loyalty and kindness in a world of scheming.

Key Fact

Shakespeare creates a spectrum of moral response: Gonzalo (consistently virtuous), Alonso (sinful but repentant), and Antonio (sinful and unrepentant). This spectrum allows the play to explore the limits of forgiveness.

practice_questions.text: How does Shakespeare use the contrast between Prospero’s treatment of Ariel and Caliban to explore the theme of power?
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Ariel is addressed with terms of approval (‘my brave spirit’) and promised freedom; Caliban is called ‘slave’ and ‘thing of darkness.’ Power operates through reward (Ariel) and punishment (Caliban). The contrast raises questions about whether obedience deserves better treatment than resistance.
Lower band (1-2): Basic observation that Prospero treats Ariel better than Caliban.

practice_questions.text: Read Caliban’s ‘isle is full of noises’ speech (Act 3, Scene 2). How does Shakespeare present Caliban as more than a ‘savage’?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (13-15) Analyses sensory imagery (‘sweet airs,’ ‘a thousand twangling instruments’), the dream of riches, and the emotional depth. The poetry contradicts Prospero’s characterisation of Caliban as ‘a born devil.’ Forces the audience to question who determines ‘civilisation.’ Postcolonial context.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses Miranda’s line ‘O brave new world’ to create dramatic irony.

practice_questions.text: How does Shakespeare use Prospero’s breaking of his staff to explore the theme of renunciation?
practice_questions.marks:

Lower band (1-2): Basic identification that Prospero gives up his magic.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses the concept of ‘the Other’ in Prospero’s characterisation of Caliban.
